c.tagline: UNESCO gastronomy capital of baklava, pistachios, and Roman mosaics.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are metered; Uber connects you to licensed metered taxis rather than private cars. Confirm the meter is running at the start of the ride.

emergency.note: 112 is Türkiye's unified emergency number, connecting to police, ambulance, and fire services.

avoid.reason: Avoid districts along the Syrian border outside the city; central Gaziantep itself is fine.
Usual pickpocket awareness in the crowded Bakırcılar coppersmith bazaar.

hood_desc: The restored historic core (Old City) of stone mansions, hans, and narrow lanes around Gaziantep Castle and the Zeugma Mosaic Museum; best for first-timers who want boutique hotels in Ottoman-era buildings within walking distance of the main sights.

The busy commercial and administrative heart of the Şahinbey district, lined with shops, restaurants, and mid-range hotels along Atatürk Boulevard; a convenient, well-connected base in the middle of the city.

Gaziantep's modern, greener northern district of wide avenues, malls, and international-brand hotels around Mücahitler and İbrahimli; suits business travelers and those wanting newer, quieter accommodation.

The atmospheric Coppersmiths' Bazaar (Bakırcılar Çarşısı) quarter and adjoining covered markets, where artisans still hammer copper and sell spices, baklava, and antiques; ideal for shoppers and food lovers.

The Castle quarter (Kaleiçi) at the foot of Gaziantep Castle, dense with traditional courtyard houses, kebab houses, and the copper and spice bazaars; a characterful, sights-heavy base close to the old town.

transit.hours: Trams and buses generally run from around 6:00 AM to midnight; Gaziray commuter trains run through the day at regular intervals.
transit.note: Gaziulaş runs the city's public transport: roughly 70 bus routes, three tram lines, and the Gaziray commuter rail crossing the city east–west. The T1 tram is the most useful line for visitors, linking the railway station area through the central districts.
transit.pay: Fares are paid with the rechargeable Gazikart smart card, tapped on board buses and trams and at Gaziray stations. Cards are sold at kiosks and station machines.

bus: Intercity coaches from Gaziantep Otogar to Şanlıurfa, Adana, and beyond
train: Gaziantep railway station (TCDD regional and sleeper services to Adana, Malatya, and connections onward)

transit.m: Municipal bus to city center (~45-60 min)

tip.r: Rounding up the bill or leaving about 5-10% for good service in restaurants is appreciated but not obligatory.

food.name: Antep Baklavasi
food.desc: Forty-plus tissue-thin layers of dough, clarified sheep butter and green Antep pistachios, baked and syruped; the citys UNESCO calling card.

places.name: Imam Cagdas
places.note: Serving baklava since 1887 in the covered bazaar; the benchmark tray in Turkey.

places.name: Kocak Baklava
places.note: Family firm from 1943 known for extra-pistachio kuru and sobiyet baklava.

places.name: Gulluoglu Gaziantep
places.note: Historic Gullu family bakery; watch the sheets rolled fresh each morning.

food.name: Beyran Corbasi
food.desc: Fiery garlic-and-chilli lamb soup with rice and shreds of slow-cooked shank, traditionally eaten at dawn as breakfast.

places.name: Metanet Lokantasi
places.note: The city standard for beyran; opens before sunrise and usually sells out by noon.

places.name: Sakip Usta Paca Beyran Kebap
places.note: Shanks and marrowbones simmered 10-12 hours; locals queue for the early service.

places.name: Cigerci Kazim Usta
places.note: Market-side breakfast spot pairing beyran with grilled liver skewers.

food.name: Katmer
food.desc: Paper-thin pastry folded around clotted kaymak and crushed pistachio, baked crisp and cut into squares; a Gaziantep breakfast sweet.

places.name: Katmerci Zekeriya Usta
places.note: Best-known katmer master in town; dough stretched to order in the window.

places.name: Orkide Pastanesi
places.note: Long-running patisserie doing katmer alongside pistachio kadayif and ice cream.

places.name: Imam Cagdas
places.note: Morning katmer served with tea in the historic bazaar dining room.

food.name: Gaziantep Lahmacun
food.desc: Wafer-thin flatbread spread with minced lamb, tomato, garlic and local pepper, fired in a wood oven and rolled with parsley and lemon.

places.name: Kebapci Halil Usta
places.note: Wood-fired lahmacun and kebabs; a reliable local favourite for decades.

places.name: Imam Cagdas
places.note: Orders its lahmacun from the same ovens that supply its kebab kitchen.

places.name: Bakircilar Carsisi bakeries
places.note: Cluster of small firin stalls selling lahmacun straight off the peel.

food.name: Yuvalama
food.desc: Festive soup of tiny rice-and-semolina dumplings with chickpeas and lamb in a tangy yoghurt broth, finished with dried mint butter.

places.name: Metanet Lokantasi
places.note: Classic tradesmen's lokanta where yuvalama appears daily in the steam trays.

places.name: Bayazhan Restaurant
places.note: Regional menu in a historic stone courtyard; good for less common Antep soups.

places.name: Ali Usta Kebap ve Baklava
places.note: Home-style Antep cooking, strong on yoghurt-based dishes and kebabs.

food.name: Ali Nazik Kebab
food.desc: Minced lamb kebab laid over smoky charred-aubergine puree beaten with garlic yoghurt; said to have been invented in Gaziantep.

places.name: Imam Cagdas
places.note: Charcoal kebabs from a 130-year-old kitchen; ali nazik is a house staple.

places.name: Kebapci Halil Usta
places.note: Generous portions and properly smoky aubergine base.

places.name: Bayazhan Restaurant
places.note: Courtyard setting near the castle, good for a sit-down kebab dinner.

food.name: Menengic Kahvesi
food.desc: Caffeine-free coffee ground from roasted wild terebinth berries and brewed with milk; nutty, thick and unique to the southeast.

places.name: Tahmis Kahvesi
places.note: Coffeehouse dating to 1635, the traditional address for menengic in Antep.

places.name: Papirus Cafe
places.note: Courtyard cafe in a historic house serving menengic and Turkish coffee.

places.name: Bayazhan Restaurant
places.note: Serves menengic after meals in its stone-arched han courtyard.

food.name: Meyan Serbeti
food.desc: Bitter-sweet licorice root sherbet shaken cold from a brass urn; a southeastern summer thirst-quencher sold by street vendors.

places.name: Elmaci Pazari vendors
places.note: Traditional urn-carrying serbetci work the market lanes through summer.

places.name: Tahmis Kahvesi
places.note: Historic cafe that also pours meyan and other traditional serbet.

places.name: Almaci Pazari stalls
places.note: Cluster of stalls selling meyan, sumac and tamarind sherbets by the glass.

landmarks: Zeugma Mosaic Museum
One of the world's great mosaic collections, its Roman masterpieces rescued from the drowned city of Zeugma include the haunting, celebrated Gypsy Girl.
Gaziantep Castle (Gaziantep Kalesi)
This circular hilltop citadel, rebuilt by Justinian atop Bronze Age foundations, has watched over Antep's bazaars for millennia and symbolizes the city's 1921 resistance.
Bakırcılar Çarşısı (Coppersmiths' Bazaar)
Hammers ring through this centuries-old covered market where artisans still beat copper trays and coffee pots by hand amid mounds of pistachios and spices.
Zincirli Bedesten
A restored 18th-century covered market hall whose vaulted stone aisles brim with baklava, dried peppers, soap and the aromas of Antep's famed cuisine.
Tahmis Kahvesi
Serving coffee since 1635, this atmospheric two-storey stone coffeehouse is the place to sip menengiç coffee where camel caravans once paused.
Hasan Süzer Ethnography Museum
A grand 19th-century courtyard mansion of carved black-and-white stone, its rooms recreated to show the daily life of a wealthy Ottoman Antep family.
Emine Göğüş Culinary Museum
Set in an 1904 stone house, this small museum lovingly documents the baklava, kebabs and pistachio culture that earned Gaziantep UNESCO gastronomy status.
Kurtuluş Mosque (Liberation Mosque)
Built in 1892 as an Armenian cathedral with striking striped stonework, this converted landmark tells the layered story of Antep's communities.
Panorama 25 Aralık Museum
A dramatic panoramic museum commemorating Gaziantep's heroic 1920-21 defense against French occupation, complete with immersive dioramas beneath the castle hill.
Rumkale (Hromgla)
A day-trippable clifftop fortress rising sheer above the turquoise Euphrates, reached by boat from Halfeti past half-submerged villages and minarets.

train.note: No international trains - the Syrian border crossings are closed to passenger rail. Gaziantep station has conventional services west toward Adana and Mersin and east to Karkamış, and a high-speed line toward Şanlıurfa and Ankara is under construction. Book on TCDD e-bilet from 15 days out; most travellers use the coach or fly.

bus.note: No reliable scheduled international coach - the Syrian border is not a normal crossing for travellers. Gaziantep's otogar runs frequent domestic services to Şanlıurfa (about 2 hours), Adana, Mardin, Ankara and Istanbul on Has Turizm, Metro Turizm (https://www.metroturizm.com.tr/en) and Öz Diyarbakır; book through obilet (https://www.obilet.com/en/).

ferry.note: Gaziantep is inland in south-eastern Anatolia with no coast, so there are no ferries.

half.name: Halfeti
half.blurb: Euphrates riverside town partly submerged by a dam, toured by boat past a half-drowned mosque minaret.

full.name: Şanlıurfa & Göbekli Tepe
full.blurb: Home to the world's oldest known monumental temple complex, plus Şanlıurfa's sacred carp pools and old bazaar.

full.name: Mount Nemrut
full.blurb: Mountaintop tomb-sanctuary ringed by giant stone heads of gods, built by a first-century BC king.
